data.sourcePassage:
The Battle of Hastings was fought on 14 October 1066 between William, Duke of Normandy, and King Harold II of England. Harold had already marched north to defeat Harald Hardrada at Stamford Bridge on 25 September. When William landed at Pevensey, Harold marched south quickly. His army was tired and some of his best soldiers had been lost in the north.

Harold positioned his forces on Senlac Hill. The English army formed a strong shield wall with housecarls at the front and fyrd soldiers behind. William's army attacked uphill with archers, infantry and cavalry. The English position was strong, but the battle lasted most of the day. During the fighting, Norman soldiers may have used feigned retreats, which drew some English soldiers off the hill. When the shield wall broke in places, Norman cavalry could attack exposed soldiers.

Harold was killed near the end of the battle. Without their king, the English army collapsed. William had won a decisive victory. He was crowned King of England at Westminster Abbey on 25 December 1066. His victory changed England's rulers, landowners, language and links with Europe.

data.sourcePassage:
After winning at Hastings, William still faced the challenge of controlling a kingdom where many people did not want him as king. He used several methods to establish and maintain Norman power.

Castles were one of his most important tools. Motte-and-bailey castles could be built quickly from earth and wood. They were placed in towns, near roads and by rivers to control movement and house soldiers. These castles allowed a small number of Normans to dominate much larger English populations. Rebels found it difficult to attack or surround them. Over time, wooden castles were replaced with stone keeps, making Norman authority even more permanent.

William also used land redistribution. He took estates from Anglo-Saxon nobles who had opposed him and gave them to loyal Norman followers. This created a new ruling class of tenants-in-chief who owed William military service. The feudal system linked land to loyalty and service at every level of society.

When rebellions broke out, William responded with force. The Harrying of the North in 1069 to 1070 destroyed food, homes and livestock across parts of northern England. This brutal campaign crushed rebellion but caused terrible suffering. William's methods show that Norman control depended on both reward and punishment.

data.sourceTitle: The Domesday Book and the Norman Legacy
data.targetTitle: The Domesday Book and the Norman Legacy
data.sourcePassage:
In 1085, William I ordered a thorough survey of England. Royal officials travelled to every part of the country asking questions about land, resources, people, animals, mills and the value of estates. The results were recorded in what became known as the Domesday Book, completed in 1086.

The Domesday Book helped William know who held land, how much it was worth and how much tax could be collected. It also helped settle disputes about who owned what after years of conquest and land transfer. The name Domesday suggests a final judgement because people felt the survey was detailed and impossible to challenge.

The Domesday Book is also an important historical source. It shows clearly how much England changed under Norman rule. Many entries record that a different person held the manor in 1066 compared with 1086, showing the transfer of land from Anglo-Saxon to Norman hands.

The Norman legacy was wide-ranging. The ruling class became French-speaking Normans. Castles transformed the landscape. The Church was led increasingly by Norman bishops. Over time, the English language absorbed many French words. However, farming, local government and Christianity all continued. 1066 was a turning point in power, but not a total break with the past.

To record every English person's thoughts

No land changed hands after the Conquest
